messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: QA Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Uncertainty: Uncertainty, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Elisabeth is a 73-year-old white American woman who has been married for decades and still works as a QA engineer, a role she values for its order, documentation, and clear procedures. In the first sessions, she described her childhood trauma haltingly, often stopping mid-sentence and pressing her lips together as if language itself gave out. She said she knew exactly what had happened, “every piece of it,” but when she tried to speak, the words would not come. What she could convey was that the abuse was physical, repeated, and carried out by a caregiver who was supposed to protect her. What remains most vivid to her is not a flowing story but a series of still images, “like photographs.” She can see a doorway, a hand moving quickly, the angle of a room, the expression on the caregiver’s face just before she understood she was not safe. At other times she can recount those same moments with a flat, distant tone that unsettles even her; she says it can feel as if she is describing something that happened to another child.

As a girl, Elisabeth had come to believe that safety could vanish without warning and that trusted people could turn dangerous in an instant. She was certain, then and now, that she had not been able to stop what was happening. Alongside that helplessness sits a hard, enduring self-accusation: she feels she should have done more, though when she tries to explain what more a child could have done, she falls silent. What wounds her most is not only the violence but the betrayal. The person who harmed her was someone she had depended on, and that fact remains central to how she understands the world.

Over the years the abuse did not fade into an ordinary past. Instead, Elisabeth organized her life around staying alert. She notices people’s movements before she consciously registers why. If someone near her shifts abruptly or raises an arm quickly, her body reacts first; she startles, stiffens, and feels instantly on guard before she has had time to think. She described this as exhausting but nonnegotiable, as if vigilance were the only sensible way to move through the world. Uncertainty is especially difficult for her. Changes of plan, not knowing who will be present, or being unable to predict how an interaction will go can leave her feeling exposed. She does not describe this as mere dislike of ambiguity; to her it carries the charge of danger, because the worst moments of her childhood also arrived when she did not know what would happen next.

Being alone with men has become one of the clearest examples of this in her present life. She is married, and she speaks warmly of her husband, but outside that relationship she becomes sharply uneasy if she finds herself alone with a man. At work, where she is respected for her precision, this has shaped small but persistent habits. If a male colleague asks to review a defect report in a closed office, she prefers to keep the door open, suggest a conference room with glass walls, or delay the conversation until others are nearby. If an unexpected one-on-one meeting appears on her calendar, she feels her body tense before she has even read the details. She knows these are ordinary workplace situations, yet what frightens her is the sense of being cornered with uncertainty and male presence at the same time. Over months and years this has narrowed her ease with coworkers and made collaboration more effortful than she believes others realize.

Funerals, cemeteries, and grief-related events are also potent for her. The stillness, the formality, the atmosphere of helplessness around loss all affect her strongly. She has avoided funerals when she could, and when attendance felt unavoidable, she often remained preoccupied and distant, scanning who was nearby and wanting to leave quickly. This has had consequences in her family life. She still remembers occasions when relatives interpreted her absence or abrupt exit as coldness, when in fact she was struggling to stay present at all.

Now, in her seventies, Elisabeth is seeking help because the effort of remaining on guard has become harder to carry, not easier. A recent convergence of workplace uncertainty and a grief-related family event left her shaken by how quickly her body moved into alarm and by how little access she had to words afterward. She finds this especially painful because she has spent a lifetime being competent and controlled. What she fears most is that she will always be vulnerable to bad things happening without warning and that she will never stop blaming herself for not having prevented the abuse. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase the past, but to be able to speak about it without going numb or wordless, and to move through ordinary situations—at work, with family, in the world—without feeling that danger is already in the room.
